newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish premier criticises striking doctors.
newsitem.headline: Polish premier criticises striking doctors.

text.p: Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz on Wednesday criticised doctors, on strike for more pay and funding for the health service, saying their protest was unethical.

"I deplore the obstinacy of the organisers of the health care strike. It can never be compatible with elementary rules of doctors' ethics," PAP news agency quoted Cimoszewicz as saying before a cabinet meeting.
The strike, launched on Monday by a union grouping one third of Poland's 90,000 doctors, has affected about two-thirds of the nation's 900 hospitals and half of its outpatient clinics.
Doctors have cancelled routine operations and examinations but continue to treat emergency cases and work at cancer, psychiatric, children's and maternity wards.

They demand increasing next year's spending for the public health care sector to six percent of gross domestic product from 4.5 percent, or nearly 20 billion zlotys ($7.1 billion), planned by the government in the national budget draft.
The doctors also seek a collective pay pact, which would increase their average monthly gross salary to about 3,000 zlotys ($1,070) -- three times the average industrial wage.

The health ministry had earlier said the demands could not be met because there was no funding for them in next year's budget and Cimoszewicz said on Wednesday the government would not boost the deficit to satisfy doctors.
"The government can take actions, which are possible within the framework of this and next year's budgets," PAP quoted him as saying.

He ruled out direct negotiations with the protesters and said talks could take place only within the so-called Trilateral Committee, a negotiating body grouping representatives of the government, trade unions and employers.
The health ministry said on Tuesday that wages of many doctors would improve after the implementation of a health care system reform, now being discussed by parliament.
The reform will introduce elements of the free market to the system, now managed centrally by the health ministry.

Although the constitution, inherited from the communist system, guarantees free medical treatment, service in state hospitals is often poor and patients must wait long periods for major surgery. Most Poles cannot afford high fees charged by private clinics, which have appeared after the fall of the old system in 1989.
